title: Separation techniques of mixture
competency: Separate mixtures using differences in size, magnetism, density, solubility and boiling point.

keywords.def: Separating the parts of a mixture by physical methods, using differences in their physical properties.
Using a magnet to separate magnetic from non-magnetic substances.
Separating particles of different sizes with a sieve.
Pouring off the top liquid layer from a solid or another liquid below.
A glass funnel with a tap, used to separate immiscible liquids.
Liquids that do not mix and form layers, like oil and water.
Removing an insoluble solid from a liquid with filter paper.
The liquid that passes through the filter paper.
The solid left behind on the filter paper.
Heating a solution so the liquid escapes and the dissolved solid stays.
Boiling a liquid and condensing its vapour to collect it.
The liquid collected after condensing in distillation.
Liquids that mix to form a solution, like alcohol and water.

ideas.name: Separation by hand, sieving and magnets

en.text: Mixtures can be separated by physical methods that use differences in their properties. Large pieces can be picked out by hand or held back by a sieve. A magnet pulls iron filings out of sand, because iron is magnetic and sand is not.

screens.title: Teff and peas
screens.ask: Your mother has teff mixed with a few peas. What is the easiest way to separate them?
opts: Pick the peas out by hand or use a sieve
screens.after:
Peas are much bigger than teff grains.
You can pick them out by hand, or shake the mix in a sieve: the small teff falls through.
Boiling, a magnet or oil would not help. Neither one is magnetic.
screens.best: Pick the peas out by hand or use a sieve

screens.title: 2.5.1 Separation techniques of mixture
paras: Most substances around us are mixtures.
Mixtures can be separated into pure substances.
Separating parts of a mixture by physical methods is a separation process.
Methods use differences in size, magnetism, melting point, boiling point and solubility.
Methods include separation by hand, sieving, filtration, evaporation, magnetic separation, decantation and distillation.

screens.title: Each method uses a difference
screens.ask: Tap each method. Which difference between the parts does it use?
items: Uses size: big pieces, like peas in teff, are picked out.
Uses particle size: small grains fall through the holes, big ones stay.
Uses magnetism: a magnet pulls iron, not sand.
Uses solubility: an insoluble solid stays on the filter paper.
Uses boiling point: the liquid escapes as vapour, the dissolved solid stays.
The solid settles, or the liquids form layers. The top liquid is poured off.
Uses boiling point: the vapour is cooled and collected as a liquid.

screens.title: I. Magnetic separation
paras: Magnetic separation separates magnetic and non-magnetic substances.
Sand mixed with iron filings is a heterogeneous mixture.
A magnet attracts the iron filings but not the sand.

screens.title: Experiment 2.4 Separation using a bar magnet
steps: Mix the sand with the iron filings on a plate.
Wrap a plastic bag around the bar magnet.
Hold the magnet over the plate. The iron collects on the magnet.
Remove the bag carefully and scrape off the iron filings.
The sand stays on the plate.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Separation process
Separating the parts of a mixture by physical methods, using differences in their physical properties.
Magnetic separation
Using a magnet to separate magnetic from non-magnetic substances.
Sieving
Separating particles of different sizes with a sieve.

screens.text: Experiment 2.4: why is the sand not attracted by the magnet?
screens.why:
A magnet attracts only magnetic substances, such as iron.
Sand is non-magnetic.
So the iron filings collect on the magnet and the sand stays on the plate.
The plastic bag only makes it easy to remove the iron afterwards.
screens.clue: What makes iron different from sand?

screens.text: Choose a separation method: how would you separate iron and charcoal?
screens.why:
Find the difference: iron is magnetic, charcoal is not.
A method that uses magnetism: magnetic separation.
Pass a magnet (in a plastic bag) over the mixture. The iron sticks; the charcoal stays.

screens.text: Sieving: a sieve with 2 mm holes is shaken over soil. What is separated, and by which property?
opts: Larger particles from fine earth, by size
Salt from water, by boiling point
screens.ans: Larger particles from fine earth, by size
screens.why:
Particles smaller than 2 mm fall through the holes: the fine earth.
Particles larger than 2 mm stay in the sieve.
What decides it is size only.
So sieving separates larger particles from fine earth, by size.
screens.clue: What decides whether a grain falls through?

en.text: Decantation separates a liquid from a settled solid, or from another liquid that does not mix, by pouring off the top layer. Clear coffee is poured from the jebena this way. Immiscible liquids like oil and water, or kerosene and water, are separated with a separating funnel: the heavier liquid runs out at the bottom.

screens.title: Jebena coffee
screens.ask: Coffee grounds sink to the bottom of the jebena. How do we get a clear cup of coffee?
opts: Pour slowly and leave the grounds behind
screens.after:
The heavy grounds settle at the bottom of the jebena.
Pour slowly and the clear coffee comes out on top, leaving the grounds behind.
Pouring off the clear liquid above a settled solid is decantation.
screens.best: Pour slowly and leave the grounds behind

screens.title: II. Decantation
paras: Decantation separates a liquid from a solid, or from an immiscible liquid.
You pour off the top liquid layer and leave the layer below.
Cooking oil and water form two layers: water at the bottom, oil on top.
Pour the oil into another vessel. The water stays behind.

screens.title: Separating funnel
paras: Liquids that do not mix form two layers. They are immiscible liquids.
A separating funnel is a glass funnel with a tap (stop-cock) in its stem.
The heavier liquid forms the lower layer; the lighter one is on top.
Open the tap to run the lower layer into a beaker. Then collect the upper layer.
Kerosene and water, and oil and water, are separated this way.

screens.title: Decanting coffee from the jebena
steps: Boil the coffee with the ground beans in the jebena.
Let it stand. The heavy grounds sink to the bottom.
Tilt the jebena slowly. Do not shake it.
The clear coffee pours out from the top: decantation.
The grounds stay behind in the jebena.

screens.caption: A funnel; a separating funnel also has a tap in its stem.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Decantation
Pouring off the top liquid layer from a solid or another liquid below.
Separating funnel
A glass funnel with a tap, used to separate immiscible liquids.
Immiscible liquids
Liquids that do not mix and form layers, like oil and water.

screens.text: Choose the apparatus: immiscible liquids can be separated by using a …
screens.why:
Immiscible liquids, like oil and water, form two layers.
A separating funnel has a tap in its stem.
Open the tap: the lower layer runs out first. Close it, then collect the upper layer.
A magnet, sieve or thermometer cannot separate two liquids.

screens.text: Separating funnel: kerosene and water are in the funnel. Which layer runs out first through the tap?
screens.why:
The heavier liquid forms the lower layer.
Water is heavier than kerosene, so water is at the bottom.
The tap is at the bottom of the funnel.
So water runs out first, and kerosene is collected after.
screens.clue: Which liquid is at the bottom?

screens.text: Two steps: muddy water is left to stand, then the clear water is poured off. Which two steps are used?
screens.why:
Step 1: while it stands, the mud settles to the bottom. That is sedimentation.
Step 2: the clear water on top is poured off. That is decantation.
No heating, filter paper or magnet is used.
So: sedimentation followed by decantation.

en.text: Filtration removes an insoluble solid from a liquid. The liquid passes through filter paper as the filtrate; the solid stays as the residue. Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from its liquid: heating drives off the liquid and the solid stays, as when salt is recovered from salt water.

screens.title: Get the salt back
screens.ask: You dissolve salt in water. How can you get the salt back?
screens.after:
Salt dissolves, so it passes through filter paper with the water.
A magnet and a sieve cannot catch dissolved salt either.
Heat the solution: the water evaporates and the salt is left.

screens.title: III. Filtration
paras: Filtration removes insoluble solids from a liquid using filter paper.
Filter paper has tiny pores that let only liquids through.
The liquid that passes through is the filtrate.
The solid left on the paper is the residue.
Chalk and water, soil and water are separated this way. Filtration helps purify tap water.

screens.title: Figure 2.21 Filtration set-up
screens.ask: Tap each part of the set-up.
items: Holds the filter paper. Pour the mixture in slowly.
Folded into a cone. Its tiny pores let only the liquid through.
The insoluble solid, like chalk or soil, left on the filter paper.
The clear liquid that passes through the paper.

screens.title: IV. Evaporation
paras: Evaporation separates a soluble solid from a liquid.
The liquid (solvent) is vaporized and the solid (solute) is left.
We separate salt from salt solution by evaporating the water.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Filtration
Removing an insoluble solid from a liquid with filter paper.
Filtrate
The liquid that passes through the filter paper.
Residue
The solid left behind on the filter paper.
Evaporation
Heating a solution so the liquid escapes and the dissolved solid stays.

screens.text: Name the method: dirty water is poured into a funnel lined with paper. Clean water comes out; dirt stays on the paper. This is …
screens.why:
The paper is filter paper: its tiny pores let only the liquid through.
The clean water that passes is the filtrate.
The dirt left on the paper is the residue.
This is filtration. Nothing is heated, so it is not evaporation or distillation.

Chalk does not dissolve → filter it off: filtration.
Salt is dissolved → evaporate the water: evaporation.
Iron is magnetic → magnetic separation.
Oil and water form layers → separating funnel.
screens.clue: Is the solid dissolved or not?
screens.text: Match each mixture to the best separation method.

screens.ask: Name the part: in filtration, the solid left on the filter paper is called the ___.
screens.why:
The liquid that passes through the paper is the filtrate.
The solid that stays on the paper is the residue.
So the answer is residue.

screens.text: Plan the order: a mixture of salt and sand must be separated. Which order works?
opts: Dissolve in water, filter, then evaporate the filtrate
screens.ans: Dissolve in water, filter, then evaporate the filtrate
screens.why:
Step 1: add water. The salt dissolves; the sand does not.
Step 2: filter. The sand stays as the residue; salt water is the filtrate.
Step 3: evaporate the filtrate. The salt is left.
Filtering the dry mixture does nothing, and neither part is magnetic.

en.text: Distillation boils a liquid and condenses its vapour in a cooled tube to collect it. It gives pure water from salt water. It also separates miscible liquids with very different boiling points: ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C, so the alcohol vaporizes first and is collected as the distillate.

screens.title: Which boils first?
screens.ask: Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C. A mixture of them is heated slowly. Which boils off first?
screens.after:
Ethanol boils at 78 °C, water at 100 °C.
As the mixture warms, it reaches 78 °C first.
So ethanol, with the lower boiling point, vaporizes first.

screens.title: V. Distillation
paras: Distillation is boiling a liquid into vapour, then condensing the vapour back to a liquid.
It is used to get pure water from salt solution.
The mixture is heated. The most volatile part vaporizes first.
The vapour passes through a cooled tube, the condenser, and becomes liquid.
The liquid collected is the distillate.

screens.title: Figure 2.23 Simple distillation set-up
items: Shows the temperature of the vapour.
A tube cooled by running water. Vapour turns back to liquid.

screens.title: Pure water from salt water, step by step
steps: Put salt water in the distilling flask and heat it with the burner.
At 100 °C the water boils and turns into vapour.
The salt does not boil. It stays in the flask.
The vapour passes into the condenser, a tube cooled by running water.
The cool tube turns the vapour back into liquid water.
Pure water, the distillate, drips into the receiving flask.

screens.title: Miscible liquids
paras: Liquids that mix to form a solution are miscible liquids.
Alcohol and water are miscible.
Ethanol boils at 78 °C; water boils at 100 °C.
On heating, the alcohol vaporizes faster and is collected as distillate.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Distillation
Boiling a liquid and condensing its vapour to collect it.
Distillate
The liquid collected after condensing in distillation.
Miscible liquids
Liquids that mix to form a solution, like alcohol and water.

screens.text: Choose a separation method: how would you separate a mixture of alcohol and water?
screens.why:
Alcohol and water are miscible: they mix, so they form no layers.
A separating funnel will not work, and nothing is magnetic or solid.
They have different boiling points: ethanol 78 °C, water 100 °C.
So use simple distillation: the alcohol boils off first and is collected.
screens.clue: They mix, so a funnel will not work.

screens.text: True or false? In distillation, the condenser cools the vapour so it turns back into a liquid.
screens.why:
Cool water runs around the condenser tube.
Hot vapour loses heat inside the tube.
It condenses: gas → liquid. The liquid is the distillate.
So the statement is true.

screens.text: Compare methods: which separation method collects BOTH the salt and the pure water from salt water?
screens.why:
Evaporation in an open dish: the salt stays, but the water vapour escapes into the air.
Distillation: the vapour is caught in the condenser and collected as pure water.
The salt stays behind in the flask.
Filtration and decantation cannot remove dissolved salt. So distillation.
screens.clue: In which method is the vapour caught?

items.title: Q1 A–D: choose a method
pairs: B. Iron filings and sulfur powder
items.why:
A: peas are much bigger than teff → by hand or sieving (size).
B: iron is magnetic, sulfur is not → magnetic separation.
C: chalk does not dissolve → filtration.
D: oil and water form layers → separating funnel.
items.clue: What is different about the two parts?
items.text: Activity 2.16 Q1 A–D: match each mixture to a separation method.

items.title: Q1 E–H: choose a method
items.why:
E: salt is dissolved → evaporate the water.
F: alcohol and water mix, but boil at different temperatures → simple distillation.
G: salt dissolves, sand does not → dissolve, filter, evaporate.
H: the fruits are big and easy to see → separate by hand.
items.text: Activity 2.16 Q1 E–H: match each mixture to a separation method.
Activity 2.18 i. How would you separate a mixture of salt, sand and water?
opts: Filter off the sand, then evaporate the filtrate
items.ans: Filter off the sand, then evaporate the filtrate
items.why:
The salt is already dissolved in the water; the sand is not.
Step 1: filter. Sand stays on the paper as the residue.
Step 2: evaporate the filtrate (salt water). The salt is left.
No part is magnetic, and there are no liquid layers.

items.text: Activity 2.18 ii. How would you separate a mixture of common salt, iron filings and sand?
opts: Magnet first, then dissolve, filter and evaporate
items.ans: Magnet first, then dissolve, filter and evaporate
items.why:
Step 1: while dry, pass a magnet over it. The iron filings are removed.
Step 2: add water. The salt dissolves; the sand does not.
Step 3: filter off the sand.
Step 4: evaporate the filtrate to get the salt.

items.text: Activity 2.18 iii. How would you separate a mixture of oil, water and sand?
opts: Filter off the sand, then use a separating funnel
items.ans: Filter off the sand, then use a separating funnel
items.why:
Step 1: filter. The sand is insoluble and stays on the filter paper.
Step 2: pour the oil and water into a separating funnel. They form two layers.
Step 3: run the lower water layer out through the tap, then collect the oil.

items.text: Activity 2.18 iv. How would you separate a mixture of sugar and clay?
opts: Dissolve, filter off the clay, gently evaporate
items.ans: Dissolve, filter off the clay, gently evaporate
items.why:
Step 1: add water. Sugar dissolves; clay does not.
Step 2: filter. The clay stays on the paper.
Step 3: gently evaporate the filtrate. The sugar is left.
Heat gently, because strong heat burns sugar. It is like salt and sand.

test.text: Choose a separation method: which method separates iron filings from sand?
test.why:
Iron is magnetic; sand is not.
A magnet pulls out the iron and the sand stays.
So use magnetic separation. Nothing here needs boiling.

test.ask: Name the part: the liquid that passes through filter paper is called the ___.
test.why:
Filter paper lets only the liquid through.
The liquid that passes is the filtrate.
The solid left behind is the residue.

test.text: Plan the order: a mixture of sand and sugar can be separated by …
opts: dissolution followed by filtration and evaporation
dissolution followed by evaporation and filtration
test.ans: dissolution followed by filtration and evaporation
test.why:
Step 1: dissolve. Add water: the sugar dissolves, the sand does not.
Step 2: filter. The sand stays on the paper.
Step 3: evaporate the filtrate. The sugar is left.
So: dissolution, then filtration, then evaporation. Evaporating before filtering would leave the sand mixed in.

test.text: Choose the apparatus: kerosene and water are best separated using a …
test.why:
Kerosene and water are immiscible: they form two layers.
A separating funnel lets the lower water layer run out through its tap.
Then the kerosene is collected.
A sieve or a magnet cannot separate two liquids.

test.text: Plan the order: iron filings, sand and salt must be separated. Which order is most appropriate?
test.why:
Step 1: magnetic separation while dry, to remove the iron.
Step 2: dissolution. Add water so the salt dissolves.
Step 3: filtration, to remove the sand.
Step 4: evaporation of the filtrate, to get the salt.
Evaporating before filtering would leave the sand with the salt.
